statement: How many different ways can three children line up one behind another?

choices.misconception: I counted the children rather than the orders they can stand in.
I multiplied three by three, which would let one child stand in two places.
I found four lines by trial and stopped before finding them all.
I thought there was only one way to make a line.

hints: Choose who goes first, then who goes next.
Decide the front of the line first: there are three choices. For each of those, two children are left for second place, and the last one has to go at the back.
Three choices for the front, then two for the middle, then one left over.

solutions.reliable: There are 3 choices for the front, then 2 for the middle, then 1 left, so 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 lines. The idea to keep: fill one place at a time and notice that each child used up is no longer available, which is why the count shrinks at each step.

whyOnTest: Listing all six lines and getting a count that matches the reasoning is how this skill is learned, and most students stop at four.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
